FEFOS v2 Validation
FEFOS v2 · Materials Project release 2026-09-28

Oxidation-state curves predict formation energies beyond binary oxides

FEFOS predicts a compound's formation energy from the binary compounds of its elements alone. This report checks that the rewritten code reproduces the 2023 paper, then tests the extension to any number of cations against every multi-cation compound in Materials Project with one of twelve anions. It then puts FEFOS against machine learning and uses it to screen for new oxides. You can also try it live below.

The idea holds and the extension works. On ionic compounds with metal cations, across all twelve anions, FEFOS predicts formation energies with a mean absolute error of eV/atom. That is half the error of the reference average without charge transfer (). The error does not grow from two cations to five or more.

Try it

This page carries FEFOS itself: the convex hulls of 891 element–anion pairs and the bond-length correction, about 70 kB. Type a formula and it runs in your browser. For compounds Materials Project reports as experimentally known, MP's own value appears alongside.

How FEFOS predicts an energy

  1. One curve per element and anion. Every binary compound MaXb sits at a formal oxidation state q = v·b/a, where v is the anion valence. The lower convex hull of formation energy against q describes how the element responds to oxidation and reduction.
  2. A common reference. All cations of a compound start at its mean oxidation state. The reference energy is the composition-weighted average of each element's hull at that state (Eq. 6 with ΔD = 0).
  3. Charge-neutral redistribution. Cations shift their oxidation states subject to Σ ci di = 0 (Eq. 2), and each shift is priced by that element's curve. The minimum is the mixing energy ΔD. Version 2 solves this exactly for any number of cations.

Three variants are compared throughout. In the linear mode the curve is the hull itself. The quadratic mode uses the paper's Eq. 1 parabolas, a1x² + a2x, fitted to the hull and weighted by concentration. The paper mode keeps the 2023 merging rule, an unweighted sum with the end-member correction of Eq. 5, generalised to n cations. In every mode the curves are fitted automatically, so the eight hand-set coefficients of 2023 are gone.

The 2023 paper, reproduced

The legacy module reruns the original binary mixing rule with the published coefficients and reference oxides. It reproduces all published predictions to within eV/atom, which is the rounding of the published table. The errors against the 2022 MP energies match the paper: eV/atom overall and for the coordination-filtered oxides. Exact agreement needed two details of the original notebook: concentrations were rounded to two decimals and snapped to a 0.02 grid, and the end-member subtraction was done separately for each oxidation direction.

The table below scores the same domain, two-cation oxides with mean oxidation state 2, 3 or 4, on today's MP energies. The published coefficients still give 0.161 eV/atom. Refitting the 2023 rule automatically to the 2026 hulls matches them without any hand tuning, and both new merging modes improve on them in every subset.

Any anion, any number of cations

The extension was scored on every multi-cation compound in MP whose most electronegative element is one of twelve anions. The fitting window for the quadratic and paper modes was chosen on the 2023 domain only and then applied unchanged everywhere else, so every result outside two-cation oxides is out of sample. The headline scope is ionic compounds with metal cations: mean oxidation state of at least 1, with no nonmetal acting as a cation.

linear quadratic paper rule reference average (no charge transfer)

What the benchmark says about the method

Charge neutrality is the right way to merge curves

Redistributing oxidation states under charge neutrality brings the error below the reference average for every anion, every cation count and every class of compound, and halves it for ionic compounds overall. This is the core FEFOS idea, and it carries over from binary oxides without change.

The exact merge is the convex hull of the binaries

With the hull itself as the curve, the charge-neutral minimum equals the energy of the most stable mixture of binary compounds. It agrees with pymatgen's phase-diagram code to 10−14 eV/atom on 394 random compounds, and its Lagrange multiplier is the anion chemical potential. The paper's parabolas are a smooth two-coefficient summary of that hull, at a cost of about 0.016 eV/atom.

Weight the curves by concentration

The 2023 rule sums the curves without concentration weights. That works for binary oxides but roughly doubles the error on bromides and iodides relative to the linear mode. Concentration weights are what thermodynamics requires, and they are the default in v2.

What is still missing

Real compounds are more stable than their binary decomposition products: the linear prediction sits eV/atom above MP on average for stable ionic compounds. Electronegativity spread explains little of this gap (r = ). Size and charge contrast from assumed bond lengths explain more, as the next section shows. Polyanions remain the main open problem.

Assumed bond lengths

The paper pointed to ionic size, through tolerance factors and the τ descriptor, as the next ingredient. FEFOS can supply sizes without the structure of the compound being predicted. Each of near-hull binary compounds gives a reference cation–anion bond length at the cation's charge. Neighbours come from CrystalNN, as in Materials Project, and charges from bond valence, so Li counts as +1 in Li2O2. Interpolating the references in charge gives an assumed bond length d(M, X, q) for any charge, across element–anion pairs. Evaluated at the oxidation states FEFOS predicts, it gives every cation a size from composition alone.

Two descriptors follow from the assumed lengths: the size mismatch of the cations (the spread of d relative to its mean) and the spread of their ionic potential q/d, an acid–base scale. Both correlate with the energy FEFOS misses, with r = and for compounds near the hull, against −0.14 for electronegativity. Compounds with more contrast are more stable than their binary decomposition products. A linear correction with three coefficients per anion (an offset and one slope per descriptor) was fitted on near-hull compounds and scored only on compounds it never saw.

FEFOS against machine learning

Composition-only machine learning is the usual alternative: Magpie descriptors with gradient boosting (Ward et al. 2016, the baseline Bartel et al. used) and attention networks such as Roost (Goodall and Lee 2020), which the 2023 paper compared against. To compare fairly, every model below sees the same data. Test compounds come from a fifth of chemical systems that are never seen in training, at any composition. Every model is also given all binary compounds, because FEFOS uses them. The question is how many multi-cation DFT calculations a learned model needs before it beats a model that needs none.

Screening for new oxides

Because FEFOS is fast, it can sweep a whole chemical space. Every pair of metal cations was combined at ratios 1:1, 1:2, 2:1, 1:3 and 3:1, with oxygen set by charge balance from each element's common oxidation states. That gives ternary oxides, of them absent from Materials Project. Each was scored by its predicted distance to the current MP hull of its A–B–O system, built from every known phase including intermetallics and known ternaries.

FEFOS alone can never place a new composition below the hull, because its prediction is the binary hull. The screen therefore uses FEFOS with the oxide bond correction and two guardrails. FEFOS's own oxidation states must agree with a charge-balanced assignment, and both bond descriptors must lie in the range seen in training. That removes artefacts such as OsO4-derived "compounds" with a noble metal at oxidation state 0. new compositions in chemical systems are predicted at least 0.10 eV/atom below the current hull, and of them are also predicted stable by the learned second opinion.

Is any of it useful for catalysis?

The shortlist falls into a few families. Each was checked against the literature; the notes below say what is known about the family in catalysis and whether the specific composition has been reported.

Alkali iridates OER

Rb2IrO3, Rb2Ir2O5, RbIrO2, Rb2Ir4O9, Cs2Ir6O13

Iridium oxides are the benchmark catalysts for oxygen evolution in acid. Li-, Na- and K-containing iridium oxides have been made from amorphous iridium oxyhydroxide and tested for OER; activity falls as the alkali gets larger while durability improves (ChemCatChem 2024). The only reported rubidium iridates are highly oxidised: Rb5Ir2O9, Rb7Ir3O12 and Rb12Ir7O24, with iridium near +5 to +6.5. They are water-sensitive and absent from MP (Inorg. Chem. 2022). The four Ir(III)/Ir(IV) compositions that pass both models are unreported. So is Rb4IrO4, the missing member of the Na/K/Cs A4IrO4 family, which FEFOS also places below the current hull. The azide/nitrate route used for Na4IrO4 (arXiv:1502.02275) is the natural way to make them. The prediction is uncertain for two reasons: MP's Rb–Ir–O hull lacks the three known phases, and the activity trend suggests Rb would be durable but not especially active.

Thallium ruthenates and iridates OER/ORR toxic

Tl2RuO3, Tl2Ru2O5, Tl2Ru6O13, Tl2Ir2O5

The pyrochlore Tl2Ru2O7 is a reported bifunctional OER/ORR catalyst for Na–air batteries (Appl. Catal. B, 2019), as is Tl2Rh2O7 (Dalton Trans., 2018). The shortlisted compositions are Tl+ relatives of that family. Thallium's toxicity makes them model systems rather than practical catalysts.

Rare-earth and cerium perrhenates deoxydehydration

Ln3ReO8, Ln(ReO4)3, LnReO5, CeRe2O9, Ce2Re2O11, Ce4Re2O15

The largest family: Re7+ paired with basic rare-earth cations, the acid–base combination the bond descriptors reward. Both models flag Ln3ReO8 for Ln = Tb, Dy, Tm and Lu. That fluorite-type family is reported experimentally for Ln = Sm to Lu (ECM abstract, TU Darmstadt thesis) but missing from MP, so these are rediscoveries. Hydrated lanthanide perrhenates are also known. ReOx dispersed on CeO2 and Ce–Zr oxides is an established deoxydehydration catalyst for biomass-derived polyols (ReOx on ceria, Re on CexZr1−xO2, 2026). No defined Ce–Re–O compound turned up, so the Ce–Re–O candidates could serve as bulk models of that interface.

Molybdates and tungstates photocatalysis

Ag2Mo4O13, Eu2Mo2O9, Eu2W2O9, Tl2W4O13

Ag2Mo4O13 is a known, synthesised visible-light photocatalyst (J. Hazard. Mater., 2011) that Materials Project does not contain; FEFOS found it from composition alone. Rare-earth molybdates are studied mostly for luminescence; no catalytic data for the europium compounds turned up.

Related ideas

  • Acid–base enthalpies. Navrotsky and co-workers relate the formation enthalpies of ternary oxides from binary oxides to the acid–base contrast of the cations, linked to the Cartledge ionic potential, charge over radius (review). For ternary nitrides the enthalpy from binaries is linear in the ionic-potential ratio of the cations (McHale et al., Chem. Mater. 1997). FEFOS's bond correction uses the same descriptor, computed from assumed bond lengths.
  • Ternary oxides from binary oxides in DFT. Hautier et al. compiled 135 reactions forming ternary oxides from binaries to test DFT accuracy, and Jain et al. calibrated the GGA/GGA+U mixing Materials Project uses on binary data (Jain et al., 2011). Those reaction energies are exactly what FEFOS's linear mode leaves out.
  • Machine-learned formation energies. Magpie descriptors (Ward et al. 2016), ElemNet, Roost (Goodall and Lee 2020) and CrabNet (Wang et al. 2021) learn from tens of thousands of compounds. Bartel et al. showed they predict formation energies well but stability poorly (npj Comput. Mater. 2020).
  • Miedema's model. The classic semi-empirical estimate for alloy formation enthalpies, extended to ternaries by energy minimisation over binaries (Mousavi et al. 2016), much as FEFOS minimises over binary hulls. It targets intermetallics and has no oxidation-state physics, so it does not apply to oxides.
